pages.title: THREE INTELLIGENCE EXPLOSIONS
pages.subtitle: Software, chips, factories: three loops, three speeds
pages.learner: Is an intelligence explosion just one thing?

panels.heading: The Core Question
panels.body:
Intelligence explosion (IE) = very fast AI progress once AI can build better AI.
Key question: which feedback loop closes, and how fast?
Forethought (Davidson, Hadshar, MacAskill, 2025) splits it into three loops.
panels.diagram: Big circular arrow: 'better AI' -> 'more and smarter AI researchers' -> 'faster AI R&D' -> back to 'better AI'. The robot tutor points at the loop; a small question mark over the arrow labeled 'how fast?'.

panels.heading: Three Feedback Loops
panels.body:
Software: AI improves algorithms, data, post-training. Lag: months.
Chip technology: AI designs better chips (more computation per dollar). Lag: many months.
Chip production: AI plus robots build and run more fabs. Lag: years.
panels.diagram: Three concentric loops of increasing size, colored cyan (software), violet (chip technology), amber (chip production). Each loop has a clock icon labeled 'months', 'many months', 'years'. Icons: code brackets, a chip blueprint, a factory with a robot arm.

panels.heading: Three Types of IE
panels.body:
Software IE: software loop alone - most sudden.
AI-technology IE: software + chip technology.
Full-stack IE: all three loops - least sudden, highest ceiling.
Expected order: software -> chip tech -> chip production.
panels.diagram: Three stacked blocks like a staircase: 'Software IE' (cyan, steep short ramp), 'AI-technology IE' (cyan+violet, medium), 'Full-stack IE' (all three colors, long tall ramp). Arrow along the bottom labeled 'expected order in time'.

panels.heading: Rough Numbers
panels.body:
Chance each loop accelerates on its own: software ~50%, chip tech ~65%, production ~80%.
Ceiling in effective compute: software ~12 OOMs; full stack ~23 OOMs on Earth's energy.
OOM = order of magnitude = 10x.
panels.diagram: Left: three probability bars (50%, 65%, 80%) in the loop colors. Right: a vertical ruler marked in powers of ten with brackets 'software ~12 OOMs' and 'full stack ~23 OOMs'. Small footnote tag: 'ignores regulation and conflict'.

panels.heading: Milestone Ladders
panels.body:
Greenblatt: 3x AI -> 10x AI -> TEDAI (top-human-expert-dominating AI).
'3x' = AI help worth all staff working 3x faster.
Cotra: adequacy -> parity -> supremacy, first in AI research, then in AI production (chips, robots, power).
panels.diagram: Two ladders side by side. Ladder A rungs: '3x AI (junior engineer)', '10x AI (median lab engineer)', 'TEDAI'. Ladder B: a 3x2 grid with rows 'AI research' and 'AI production' and columns 'adequacy', 'parity', 'supremacy', arrows showing research row crossed first.

panels.heading: Who Gains Power?
panels.body:
Software IE: owners of chips and algorithms; power can concentrate fast.
AI-technology IE: adds the chip supply chain and its host countries.
Full-stack IE: adds the industrial base (energy, mining, construction); power spreads to more players.
panels.diagram: Three pie charts growing in slice count: one big slice 'chip + algorithm owners'; then added slice 'semiconductor supply chain'; then added slices 'energy', 'mining', 'construction'. Label under them: 'more loops -> power more spread out'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Three loops is a simplification; each splits further.
Lags can shrink as AI speeds up R&D.
Strategy often assumes only the rapid scenario; gradual and bumpy paths matter too.
Odds above ignore regulation and conflict.
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel with three mini curves of progress over time: 'gradual' (smooth upward bend), 'bumpy' (fast rise, plateau, rise again), 'rapid' (near-vertical). A red sticky note: 'don't plan for only one'.

panels.heading: Discuss
panels.body:
Which milestone should we track: 3x R&D speedup, full AI R&D automation, or expert-dominating AI?
If a software IE fizzles after ~3 OOMs, what changes for policy?
panels.diagram: Learner and robot at a whiteboard with three milestone cards pinned up and a question mark; one card circled in cyan.

pages.footer: Software moves first and fastest; chips and factories raise the ceiling.
pages.summary: Explains Forethought's three feedback loops (software, chip technology, chip production) and the three intelligence explosions they create, with rough odds, ceilings, power implications and milestone ladders from Greenblatt and Cotra.

sources.title: Three Types of Intelligence Explosion (Davidson, Hadshar & MacAskill, Forethought)
A breakdown of AI capability levels focused on AI R&D labor acceleration (Ryan Greenblatt)
Six milestones for AI automation (Ajeya Cotra, Planned Obsolescence)

pages.title: SOFTWARE INTELLIGENCE EXPLOSION
pages.subtitle: Does automated AI research speed itself up?
pages.learner: Will AI research snowball once AIs do it?

panels.heading: The Question
panels.body:
Software intelligence explosion (SIE) = AI improves AI software alone, with hardware fixed, and progress accelerates.
Trigger: ASARA = AI systems for AI R&D automation, able to replace every human AI researcher.
panels.diagram: A lab with a fixed rack of chips padlocked 'hardware fixed'; human researchers' desks being taken over by many robot copies. Caption arrow 'ASARA arrives'.

panels.heading: The Feedback Loop
panels.body:
Better software -> more and smarter AI researchers on the same chips -> faster software progress -> better software.
Brake: ideas get harder to find.
Which force wins?
panels.diagram: Tug of war: on the cyan side a loop labeled 'more AI researchers'; on the orange side a rope labeled 'ideas get harder to find'. A gauge in the middle reading 'r'.

panels.heading: The Key Number r
panels.body:
r = software doublings per doubling of cumulative research effort.
r > 1: each doubling comes faster (explosion).
r = 1: steady exponential.
r < 1: progress slows (fizzle).
panels.diagram: Plot of software level vs time with three curves from the same start: r > 1 bending up to near-vertical (lime), r = 1 straight on a log scale (cyan), r < 1 flattening (orange).

panels.heading: Worked Example
panels.body:
Start: software doubles in 1 month.
r = 0.7: next doublings take 41, 55, 74, 100 days.
r = 3: next doublings take 19, 12, 7.6, 4.8 days.
Same start, opposite futures.
panels.diagram: Two timelines of doubling blocks. Top (orange, r = 0.7): blocks getting wider, labeled 41, 55, 74, 100 days. Bottom (lime, r = 3): blocks shrinking, labeled 19, 12, 7.6, 4.8 days. Shared start block '30 days'.

panels.heading: Evidence on r
panels.body:
Epoch: chess engines r ~0.83; other software fields estimate above 1 but noisy.
Eth & Davidson: r ~1-4 overall, ~0.5-2 once hardware is held fixed.
Forethought model median 1.2: ~60% chance of acceleration.
panels.diagram: Number line from 0 to 4 with a bold threshold at r = 1. Dots and error bars: 'chess 0.83', 'vision ~1.4', 'model median 1.2'. Shaded band 0.5-2 labeled 'hardware fixed'.

panels.heading: No Singularity, Still Fast
panels.body:
Greenblatt (Redwood): even with r < 1, full automation gives a one-time jump.
With r = 0.7: roughly 2.5-3.5 years of progress in the first year.
Compute also gets more valuable: it now buys more AI researchers.
panels.diagram: Step chart: a flat-ish line labeled 'human researchers' then a tall step up at 'full automation' labeled '~3 years in 1 year', then continuing at a steeper slope. Small inset: chip icon turning into many robot workers.

panels.heading: Pitfalls and Bottlenecks
panels.body:
Compute bottleneck: experiments still need chips.
New frontier training runs take months.
Earlier AIs may already pick the low-hanging fruit.
r estimates come from chess, vision and SAT solvers, not AI R&D itself.
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel with icons: a queue of experiments waiting at one GPU, an hourglass labeled 'training run', a picked-over fruit tree, a magnifier over a tiny chess board labeled 'proxy data'.

panels.heading: Discuss
panels.body:
If software doubled every few days, which safeguards must already exist?
Eth & Davidson suggest measuring software progress and not exceeding ~5x the recent pace without precautions.
What early signal would show r > 1?
panels.diagram: Speedometer labeled 'software progress vs recent pace' with a red line at '5x' and a checklist beside it: security, monitoring, oversight.

pages.footer: Explosion or fizzle hinges on r - and even a fizzle can be fast.
pages.summary: Teaches the software intelligence explosion argument: once AI automates AI research, the returns parameter r decides whether progress accelerates or fizzles, what the evidence on r says, and why full automation is a big speedup even without a singularity.

sources.title: Will AI R&D Automation Cause a Software Intelligence Explosion? (Eth & Davidson, Forethought)
Full automation of AI R&D probably yields a large speed up even without a software-only singularity (Ryan Greenblatt, Redwood Research)
Do the returns to software R&D point towards a singularity? (Erdil, Besiroglu & Ho, Epoch AI)
How quick and big would a software intelligence explosion be? (Davidson & Houlden, Forethought)

pages.title: TAKEOFF MODELS CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Three models, their knobs, and what they predict
pages.learner: Why do takeoff forecasts disagree so much?

panels.heading: What a Takeoff Model Does
panels.body:
Inputs: compute growth, software progress, AI speedup of research.
Output: when milestones arrive and how fast one leads to the next.
Shared currency: effective compute = FLOP x algorithmic efficiency, recently ~10x per year.
panels.diagram: Machine diagram: three input hoppers ('compute growth', 'software progress', 'AI research speedup') feeding a box labeled 'model', which prints a timeline ribbon with milestone flags.

panels.heading: Compute-Centric Framework
panels.body:
Davidson (2023): time from AI that can automate 20% of cognitive tasks to 100%.
Gap: ~10,000x more effective compute.
Result: ~50% chance under 3 years, ~25% under 1 year (if AGI comes by 2100).
panels.diagram: S-curve of 'share of cognitive tasks automatable' vs effective compute, with markers at 20% and 100% and a bracket '~4 OOMs' between them; a timer showing 'median ~3 years'.

panels.heading: AI Futures Model (Dec 2025)
panels.body:
Stages: Automated Coder (AC) -> Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) -> superintelligence (ASI).
Stage 1 extends the METR time-horizon trend.
Lifland: AC median ~2032; ~30% chance AC to ASI takes under 1 year.
panels.diagram: Three-stage railway: station 'AC' (coding automated), station 'SAR' (research taste automated), station 'ASI'. A METR trend line feeds the first track; a calendar flag '2032 (median)' at AC.

panels.heading: Forethought SIE Model
panels.body:
Starts at ASARA with compute held fixed.
Knobs: initial speedup (median 8x), returns r (median 1.2), distance to limits (6-16 OOMs), parallel-labor penalty p.
Result: >=3 years of progress in 1 year ~60%; >=10 years ~20%.
panels.diagram: Control panel with four dials labeled 'speedup 8x', 'r 1.2', 'limits 6-16 OOMs', 'p 0.3', and an output screen showing two bars: '3 yrs in 1: ~60%' and '10 yrs in 1: ~20%'.

panels.heading: Worked Example: One Rule
panels.body:
Each software doubling takes the last one times 2^(p(1/r - 1)).
r = 1.2, p = 0.3: factor ~0.97, doublings slowly speed up.
r = 0.8, p = 0.3: factor ~1.05, doublings slow down.
panels.diagram: Two short chains of doubling bars: lime chain shrinking slightly (factor 0.97), orange chain growing slightly (factor 1.05), with the formula card above them.

panels.heading: Compare the Models
panels.body:
Compute-centric: whole economy, compute plus investment.
AI Futures: coding -> research taste -> ASI, compute keeps growing.
Forethought: software only, compute fixed (conservative).
Shared crux: does each doubling get easier or harder?
panels.diagram: Three-column comparison table with rows 'scope', 'compute', 'key knob'. Bottom banner: 'crux: each doubling faster or slower?' with arrows.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Garbage in, garbage out: trust one significant figure.
Models assume smooth trends, so they miss paradigm shifts and stalls.
Capability is squeezed into one number.
Hardware and robot automation are mostly left out.
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel: a funnel with 'garbage in' at top and 'garbage out' at bottom; a smooth curve with a hidden cliff and a hidden jump marked '?'.

panels.heading: Try It Yourself
panels.body:
Use the models' web apps with your own r and initial speedup.
What median takeoff do you get?
Which single parameter moves your answer most?
panels.diagram: Learner using a tablet with sliders labeled 'r' and 'speedup'; a histogram of takeoff durations updates on screen while the robot points at the tallest bar.

pages.footer: A takeoff forecast is only as good as its returns and bottleneck assumptions.
pages.summary: Compares three takeoff models (Davidson's compute-centric framework, the AI Futures Model Dec 2025 update, and Forethought's software intelligence explosion model), their key parameters, headline results and shared limitations.

sources.title: AI Futures Model: Dec 2025 update (AI Futures Project)
What a Compute-Centric Framework Says About Takeoff Speeds (Tom Davidson, Open Philanthropy / Coefficient Giving)
How quick and big would a software intelligence explosion be? (Davidson & Houlden, Forethought)

pages.title: MEASURING AI PROGRESS
pages.subtitle: Capability indexes, time horizons, and their blind spots
pages.learner: How do we know AI improves this fast?

panels.heading: Why Measure
panels.body:
Single benchmarks saturate within a year or two.
Forecasts need a long-running yardstick.
Two popular ones: Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) and the METR time horizon.
panels.diagram: A pile of 'maxed out' benchmark thermometers at 100%; beside them a long ruler labeled 'yardstick for years' with two tags: 'ECI' and 'time horizon'.

panels.heading: ECI: Stitch Benchmarks
panels.body:
Combines 50+ benchmarks on one scale.
Estimates each benchmark's difficulty from models tested on several.
Anchors: Claude 3.5 Sonnet = 130, GPT-5 = 150.
Only differences between models mean something.
panels.diagram: Many benchmark strips of different lengths being stitched into one long ribbon with a scale; markers at 130 and 150. Small note: 'harder benchmark -> more points'.

panels.heading: Time Horizon: Human Minutes
panels.body:
50% time horizon = length of task, in skilled-human time, an AI completes half the time.
It measures human-equivalent effort, not how long the AI runs.
Long-run trend: doubling every ~6-7 months; ~3.5-4 months in 2025.
panels.diagram: Logistic curve of AI success rate vs human task length (log scale: 1 min, 1 h, 1 day). Dashed line at 50% hitting the curve, labeled 'time horizon'. Inset: log-scale chart of horizons rising in a straight line over years.

panels.heading: Worked Example
panels.body:
Claude Opus 4.5: 50% horizon ~4 h 49 min.
95% interval: ~1 h 49 min to ~20 h.
Error bars ~2x each way, wider as the task suite saturates.
The trend slope matters more than one point.
panels.diagram: A single dot at 4h49m on a log axis with a wide error bar from 1h49m to 20h; behind it a faint trend line through many earlier dots.

panels.heading: ECI vs Time Horizon
panels.body:
ECI: broad (math, code, knowledge), relative units, harder to interpret.
Time horizon: intuitive human-time units, mostly software tasks, ~170 tasks.
At launch, +5 ECI roughly matched one horizon doubling.
panels.diagram: Two-column comparison card: left 'ECI' with a wide fan of benchmark icons; right 'Time horizon' with a stopwatch and code icon. Arrow between: '+5 ECI ~ 2x horizon'.

panels.heading: Task Mix Changes Answers
panels.body:
Greenblatt (2026): on easy-to-verify coding tasks, horizons may be ~20x METR's.
AIs write their own tests and iterate for days.
Visual computer-use horizons run 40-100x shorter.
panels.diagram: Three bars of time horizon on a log axis: 'easy-to-verify coding' (very tall, lime), 'METR suite' (medium, cyan), 'visual computer use' (short, orange).

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
50% success is not safe to delegate; many jobs need 98%+ reliability.
Benchmark tasks are clean, low-context and self-contained.
Human baseline choices shift results.
Extrapolating to month-long horizons is very uncertain.
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel: a coin flip labeled '50%' next to a bridge labeled 'needs 99%'; a neat test tube vs a messy real office desk.

panels.heading: Check Yourself
panels.body:
Model A horizon: 4 h. Model B: 5 h. Both have ~2x error bars.
Is B clearly better?
Answer: not from this alone - small gaps are noise; compare trends across many models.
panels.diagram: Two overlapping error bars on a log axis labeled A and B; the learner squints, the robot holds a sign 'look at the slope'.

pages.footer: Track the slope, respect the error bars, and ask which tasks were measured.
pages.summary: Compares Epoch's Capabilities Index and METR's time horizon as yardsticks for AI progress, with a worked example of error bars and the main limitations, including why task mix and reliability thresholds change the answer.

sources.title: Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) Documentation (Epoch AI)
Clarifying limitations of time horizon (Thomas Kwa, METR)
AIs can now often do massive easy-to-verify SWE tasks (Ryan Greenblatt, Redwood Research)

pages.title: THE CASE FOR LONG TIMELINES
pages.subtitle: Why some experts expect decades, not years
pages.learner: What if transformative AI takes decades?

panels.heading: The Question
panels.body:
Will transformative AI arrive in ~5 years or 20+?
Short-timeline views extrapolate capability trends.
Long-timeline views stress diffusion, cost and real-world friction.
panels.diagram: A fork in a road: left sign '~5 years (capability trends)', right sign '20+ years (diffusion, friction)'. Learner stands at the fork.

panels.heading: Revenue, Not Benchmarks
panels.body:
Erdil (Epoch, 2025): median ~20 years to automate remote work; ~30% within 10.
Revenue is the trend to watch, and growth may slow ~30% per doubling, like the dot-com era.
Any slowdown -> multi-decade timelines.
panels.diagram: Chart of revenue on a log scale: a straight exponential line (dashed) vs a bending curve that flattens, labeled 'slows 30% per doubling'. Small inset: dot-com revenue curve flattening after 2000.

panels.heading: Moravec's Paradox
panels.body:
AI wins most where humans are weakest (arithmetic), least where humans excel (agency, perception).
AI research is messy and bottlenecked by compute and data.
Erdil: ~10% chance of a software-driven speedup within a decade.
panels.diagram: Bar chart of AI speed advantage over humans on a log scale: 'arithmetic: billions x', 'translation: ~1,000x', 'agentic research: <10x'.

panels.heading: AI as Normal Technology
panels.body:
Narayanan & Kapoor: invention -> innovation -> adoption -> diffusion, each with a speed limit.
Aug 2024: 40% of US adults used generative AI, but only 0.5-3.5% of work hours.
Electric dynamos took ~40 years to pay off.
panels.diagram: Four-stage pipeline with funnels narrowing: 'invention', 'innovation', 'adoption', 'diffusion', each with a speed-limit sign. Below: a vintage dynamo with '~40 years' tag.

panels.heading: The Speed Limit Debate
panels.body:
Narayanan: real-world feedback caps speed; gradual adoption gives warning.
Cotra: progress could happen inside AI companies within a few years, before outsiders feel it.
Crux: do skills transfer from code and simulations to messy tasks?
panels.diagram: Split panel: left, a long gentle ramp labeled 'gradual, visible'; right, a closed lab building with a steep curve inside labeled 'fast, internal'. A bridge between labeled 'transfer?'.

panels.heading: Broad Timelines
panels.body:
Ord (2026): hold a wide distribution; his median ~2038, 80% interval 3 to 100 years.
About 1 in 5 chance within five years.
Greenblatt's reply: still focus on short timelines - more leverage, and the work transfers.
panels.diagram: A wide, right-skewed probability curve over years 2026-2126 with a marker at 2038 (median) and a shaded first-five-years slice labeled '~20%'. A smaller sharp spike labeled '2027?' crossed out.

panels.heading: Pitfalls in Both Camps
panels.body:
Short camp: treating benchmark wins as job automation.
Long camp: assuming linear revenue or past diffusion speeds must hold.
Both: compressing a distribution into a single year.
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel with two characters on a seesaw labeled 'short' and 'long', each holding a flawed sign; a calendar with one year circled and a red X.

panels.heading: Discuss
panels.body:
Which evidence would move you most: revenue per chip, lab uplift studies, or time horizons?
What work pays off in both a 5-year and a 30-year world?
panels.diagram: Robot holds three evidence cards: 'revenue per chip', 'uplift studies', 'time horizons'; learner sorts them on a balance scale.

pages.footer: Hold a broad timeline: act on short ones, plan for long ones.
pages.summary: Lays out the strongest arguments for multi-decade AI timelines (revenue trends, Moravec's paradox, diffusion speed limits, AI as normal technology), the replies from short-timeline proponents, and why a broad timeline distribution is the honest stance.

sources.title: The case for multi-decade AI timelines (Ege Erdil, Epoch AI Gradient Updates)
Does AI Progress Have a Speed Limit? (Ajeya Cotra and Arvind Narayanan, Princeton CITP)
Broad Timelines (Toby Ord, LessWrong)
AI as Normal Technology (Narayanan & Kapoor, Knight First Amendment Institute)

pages.title: COMPUTE SCALING AND UPLIFT
pages.subtitle: How far scaling goes, and measuring lab speedups
pages.learner: Can scaling continue, and does AI really help?

panels.heading: The Scaling Engine
panels.body:
Frontier training compute has grown ~4x per year.
GPT-4 used ~2e25 FLOP (floating-point operations), per Epoch.
Two questions: can this continue to 2030, and does AI speed up the labs themselves?
panels.diagram: Rocket labeled 'training compute' climbing a log-scale ladder marked 1e23, 1e25, 1e27, 1e29; a flag at 2e25 'GPT-4'. Exhaust labeled '4x per year'.

panels.heading: Four Limits to 2030
panels.body:
Power: 1-5 GW campuses -> ~1e28-3e29 FLOP; likely binds first.
Chips: ~100M H100-equivalents -> ~9e29.
Data: multimodal tokens -> ~6e28-2e32.
Latency wall: ~3e30-1e32.
panels.diagram: Horizontal log-scale bar chart of the four constraints' feasible ranges (power, chips, data, latency) with a vertical dashed line at 2e29 labeled 'Epoch central'.

panels.heading: Worked Example
panels.body:
Epoch (2024): ~2e29 FLOP runs likely feasible by 2030.
2e29 / 2e25 = 10,000x GPT-4, about the GPT-2 to GPT-4 jump.
Price tag: hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure.
panels.diagram: Equation card '2e29 / 2e25 = 1e4' next to two stacked cubes, a tiny one 'GPT-4' and a huge one '2030 run', with a dollar-sign power plant behind.

panels.heading: Is It Getting Pricier?
panels.body:
Worry: per-task inference costs keep rising.
Woodruff (Redwood, 2026): cost ratio = AI cost / human cost for the same task.
At each model's 50% horizon it stays ~3%.
Fixed-budget horizons still double every ~3 months.
panels.diagram: Scatter of successive models over time: cost ratio flat near 3% (lime line) while task length rises steeply (cyan line). Label 'longer tasks, not pricier work'.

panels.heading: Uplift: Four Measures
panels.body:
Serial speedup: how much faster staff would work without AI to match. Most useful.
Parallel: how many extra staff to match.
Current-work speedup: last week's work without AI.
Share of code written by AI: hard to convert.
panels.diagram: Four labeled gauges in a row; the 'serial speedup' gauge is highlighted in cyan with a star, the 'share of code' gauge has a question mark.

panels.heading: Worked Example: A 4x Claim
panels.body:
A 2026 lab system card reported ~4x survey uplift.
Greenblatt's simple model: 4x serial speedup -> only ~1.75x overall AI progress, since compute also matters.
His estimate of the real serial speedup: ~1.5x.
panels.diagram: Funnel: '4x serial labor' enters, mixed with a fixed 'compute' input, exits as '~1.75x AI progress'. Side note bubble: 'his estimate: ~1.5x'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Feasible is not inevitable: scaling is an investment choice.
Productivity surveys mix up serial, parallel and share-of-work.
AI doing 90% of the work is not 10x faster.
Selection effects can make costs look cheap.
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel: a pie chart '90% AI' next to a stopwatch showing only '2x'; a bag of money with a question mark labeled 'will they invest?'.

panels.heading: Check Yourself
panels.body:
Engineers say AI writes 80% of their code. Is that a 5x speedup?
Answer: not necessarily - review, design and waiting can dominate. Ask how much faster you would need to work without AI.
panels.diagram: Learner holding a sign '80% of code'; robot holding a stopwatch labeled 'serial speedup?' with a magnifier over a 'review + design' block.

pages.footer: Scaling is feasible but costly; judge uplift by serial speedup, not hype.
pages.summary: Covers Epoch's analysis of whether 4x-per-year compute scaling can continue to 2030, Redwood's evidence that AI capability gains have not come from rising costs, and how to measure AI uplift inside AI labs correctly.

sources.title: Can AI Scaling Continue Through 2030? (Sevilla et al., Epoch AI)
AI's capability improvements haven't come from it getting less affordable (Anders Cairns Woodruff, Redwood Research)
If Mythos actually made Anthropic employees 4x more productive, I would radically shorten my timelines (Ryan Greenblatt, Redwood Research)

pages.title: THE INDUSTRIAL EXPLOSION
pages.subtitle: When robot factories build robot factories
pages.learner: Could robots really double every year?

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body:
Industrial explosion = rapid growth in physical capability through a loop: robot factories build better robot factories.
Davidson & Hadshar (Forethought, 2025), a rough research note.
It follows the intelligence explosion.
panels.diagram: Loop diagram: a robot factory producing robots that build a second, larger factory, arrow back to the start. Small tag 'after the intelligence explosion'.

panels.heading: Why Later and Slower
panels.body:
Physical tasks are varied, data-poor and full of real-world friction.
Robot efficiency doubles every ~1-4 years (chips ~2, algorithms ~1).
Copying an AI takes days; building millions of robots takes years.
panels.diagram: Race track: a digital AI copy icon zooming ahead labeled 'bits: days'; a robot on a slower track labeled 'atoms: years'.

panels.heading: Three Stages
panels.body:
1) AI-directed human labor: AI coaches workers; output up ~10x.
2) Autonomous robot factories replace human physical labor.
3) Nanotechnology: smaller machines replicate faster.
panels.diagram: Three-step staircase: worker with an AI earpiece; a dark factory full of robot arms; a microscope view of tiny machines.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Payback
panels.body:
Humanoid robot: costs ~$100k, produces ~$240k of output per year.
Payback: ~5 months.
Add factory and speed costs -> robot stock doubles every ~1-2 years at first.
Today's robot stock: last doubling took ~6 years.
panels.diagram: Receipt-style card: 'cost $100k', 'output $240k/yr', '100/240 x 12 = 5 months'. Below, a doubling timeline: 'today: 6 yrs' vs 'autonomous: 1-2 yrs'.

panels.heading: Acceleration Curve
panels.body:
Experience curves: more production -> lower cost.
Growth rate may double every 1-5 doublings.
Biology hints at limits: fruit flies double in days, rats in ~6 weeks.
Long run: doubling in days or weeks.
panels.diagram: Log-scale robot population curve bending upward, with doubling-time labels shrinking: '2 yrs', '1 yr', 'months', 'weeks'. Silhouettes of a rat and a fruit fly at the top as 'biological proof of concept'.

panels.heading: Physical Limits
panels.body:
Binding constraint: energy, not materials.
5% of sunlight reaching Earth (~2e17 W) at ~100 W per robot -> ~1e14 robots.
That is many orders of magnitude above today's fleet.
panels.diagram: Sun with an arrow '2e17 W', a 5% slice routed to a crowd of robots labeled '~100 W each', result box '~1e14 robots'.

panels.heading: Strategic Stakes
panels.body:
A fast leader could gain a decisive economic and military edge.
AI takeover gets easier once AI runs physical infrastructure.
More energy and chips feed back into AI progress (full-stack IE).
panels.diagram: Two-way arrow between an 'industrial explosion' factory and an 'intelligence explosion' brain-chip; beside it a balance of power scale tipping toward one side.

panels.heading: Pitfalls and Discuss
panels.body:
Robot learning curves are poorly measured.
Regulation and human choice can slow automation.
Discuss: which places could build fastest, and what would slow them?
panels.diagram: Orange warning half: a blurry chart labeled 'robot learning curve?'. Cyan discuss half: a world map with question marks over industrial regions.

pages.footer: Bits explode first; atoms follow slower, with a far higher ceiling.
pages.summary: Explains Forethought's industrial explosion: how AI-directed labor, autonomous robot factories and eventually nanotechnology could make physical capability grow rapidly, with payback numbers, doubling-time estimates, energy limits and strategic stakes.
